analysis.one_liner: Makes war-zone fraud and overcharging the government a federal crime carrying up to 20 years in prison.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with no cosponsors, was referred to the House Judiciary Committee, received one hearing on April 1, 2009, and never got a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have created a new federal crime of war profiteering: knowingly defrauding the United States, or materially overcharging it for goods and services, on overseas military, relief, or reconstruction missions. It allowed fines up to $1 million and prison terms up to 20 years, let prosecutors bring cases in any U.S. district, allowed seizure of profits, and made the crime a trigger for money-laundering and racketeering charges. It was never voted on and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers, who fund overseas military, relief, and reconstruction contracts, would gain a stronger criminal tool against contractors who inflate prices or falsify records — including seizure of fraud proceeds and racketeering charges against repeat offenders.

how_it_helps.text: It would make it a federal crime, punishable by up to 20 years and a $1 million fine, to defraud the United States or a provisional authority on overseas missions, including materially overvaluing goods or services with intent to defraud.

It would extend federal jurisdiction extraterritorially and allow prosecution in any district where an act took place or a contractor is located, closing the gap that previously let overseas war-zone fraud escape easy prosecution.
It would allow criminal forfeiture of property gained from war profiteering and would make the offense a predicate for money-laundering and racketeering (RICO) prosecutions.

analysis.who_pays: Defense, logistics, and reconstruction contractors doing overseas work for the U.S. government would bear new criminal exposure, forfeitures, and prosecution anywhere a U.S. district has a connection.

drawbacks.text: The bill would expand federal criminal jurisdiction and increase penalties (up to 20 years) for conduct — fraud and misrepresentation on government contracts — that existing fraud and False Claims Act laws already punish, raising a risk of overlapping prosecution.

Defining 'materially overvaluing' goods and services with intent to defraud could reach borderline pricing disputes on wartime contracts, and the broad venue and extraterritorial provisions could expose contractors to prosecution in any U.S. district where they do business.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: On its face, the bill's benefits — stronger penalties for defrauding taxpayers on overseas contracts and closing loopholes that let war-zone fraud escape U.S. courts — outweigh the costs, which are limited to the price of prosecution and a modest expansion of federal criminal jurisdiction. The bill's fatal weakness was procedural, not substantive: it drew no cosponsors and no committee action beyond one hearing, so its merits were never tested in markup or on the floor.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, referred to the House Judiciary Committee, got a single hearing, and then sat there until the Congress ended without ever reaching a vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Neil Abercrombie introduced the bill on March 23, 2009, and it was referred to the House Judiciary Committee the same day.
No other member signed on as a cosponsor.
The committee held a hearing on April 1, 2009 — the bill's only recorded action after referral — and no markup or floor vote ever followed.
The bill died in committee when the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Defense and reconstruction contractors who might have been prosecuted for wartime fraud are better off, since no new penalties were enacted. Taxpayers lost the chance at a stronger remedy.

for.name: Rep. Neil Abercrombie
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and its sole advocacy in the record; it drew no cosponsors.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Held a single hearing on the bill and never scheduled a markup or reported it to the floor.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never advanced far enough for a party split to show; it had no cosponsors of either party.

industries.industry: Government contractors operating in war zones (defense, logistics, reconstruction, security firms)
industries.note: The bill would expose contractors on overseas U.S. missions to a new criminal offense with 20-year maximum sentences, asset forfeiture, RICO and money-laundering exposure, and prosecution in any U.S. district. It died, so contractors face no new penalties.
Legitimate firms would face new criminal-law exposure and heavier compliance costs, though the law would only punish knowing fraud or deliberate overvaluation, not ordinary business judgment.
